meta.name: Seattle (downtown and Seattle Center)
meta.scaleNote: game units per real metre; uniform, no compression
meta.originNote: centre of the play box: First Ave at about Union St, by the Seattle Art Museum
meta.coverage: South edge at T-Mobile Park, north to the south shore of Lake Union, west into Elliott Bay past the piers, east to I-5 (the foot of First Hill and Capitol Hill). 586 x 889 u (2.9 x 4.4 km).
meta.terrain: FLAT. Seattle is steep (the downtown core climbs about 40 m from the waterfront to Fifth Ave and I-5; Pike Place Market and the Belltown bluff stand above Alaskan Way); the game ground is flat and the hills are not modelled. Heights are measured from each building's own ground.
meta.axes: +X = east, -Z = north (true north up), +Y up. Matches the minimap (screen up = -Z).
meta.gridNote: Three street grids meet downtown and are kept: cardinal (Pioneer Square south of Yesler Way, the International District, SoDo, Seattle Center, South Lake Union); core (Yesler to Stewart St: avenues 32 deg west of north, cross streets bearing 58 deg; street-aligned rot about 0.559); belltown (Belltown and the Denny Triangle: avenues 49 deg west of north, rot about 0.855). Landmark front = compass point of frontBearing (deg clockwise from north) and frontDir = the world (x, z) unit vector; grid = the landmark's grid.
meta.rotNote: All rot values are three.js rotation.y (radians). An object rotated by rot has its local +X axis pointing along (cos rot, -sin rot) in world (x, z). Building w is along local X, d along local Z: footprints on the rotated grids are oriented rects (OBB), not axis-aligned.
meta.footprintNote: Footprints are CCW viewed from above (CCW in (x, -z)), open rings (first vertex not repeated). For THREE.Shape use (x, -z) then rotateX(-PI/2).
meta.heightNote: height / eaveHeight are game units (metres x 0.2). Landmarks: heightMetres = top of the structure incl. spires and masts; eaveMetres = main roof, or where the crown begins; dataRoofMetres = the outline data's height of the matched footprint. Buildings: heightMetres = Seattle 2015 roof apex elevation minus the 3DEP bare-earth ground at the roof part (the height the top 35% of the roof area reaches), OSM height for buildings newer than 2015, else the neighbours' median; a merged block mass takes the area-weighted height and keeps heightMaxMetres.
meta.mergeNote: Inside each street block (a face of the road network), touching buildings under 60 m within 1.8x of each other in height are merged while their union fills at least 62% of its rectangle and no side passes 110 m; slivers under 700 m2 fold into the nearest-height neighbour. A tower standing on a podium in the data is split into the tower (its own entry) and the podium (podiumOf = the tower's id). footprint = the outline; cx/cz/w/d/rot = its oriented rectangle (what the kit fills); phoneSkip = small low structures that touch no street.
meta.buildingFields: bin = the City of Seattle 2023 outline OBJECTID (o<id>, t = tower part, p<n> = podium part, synth: = synthesised); onPier = stands on a pier or over Elliott Bay (keep it, do not drop it as in-water); zone = pike_place / pioneer_square / international_district / sodo / seattle_center / south_lake_union / belltown / denny_triangle / core; style (generic only) = brick (historic brick and terracotta, 1890-1930: Pioneer Square, the ID, the Market, low Belltown), warehouse (pier sheds, SoDo / port sheds), lowrise (< 15 m commercial), midrise (15-60 m concrete and glass offices), apartment (15-60 m modern residential mid-rise with coloured panels and balconies: Belltown, Denny Triangle, South Lake Union), glassslab (60-120 m glass slab), glasstower (120 m and more); frontage = avenue / street.
meta.projection: equirectangular about origin: x = (lon-lon0)*75188.2*scale, z = -(lat-lat0)*111182.7*scale (WGS84 metres per degree at lat0)
meta.source: City of Seattle open data (Seattle GeoData, ArcGIS feature services): Building Outlines 2023 (footprints), Building Outlines 2015 (roof parts with BP99_APEX roof apex elevations), SDOT Trees (street trees). USGS 3DEP 1 m bare-earth DEM (elevation.nationalmap.gov) for ground elevation under each roof. OpenStreetMap contributors, ODbL 1.0 (https://www.openstreetmap.org/copyright), Overpass API snapshot 2026-11-15/16: coastline, Lake Union, roads, parks, paths, piers, bridges, rail and the Monorail, building names and heights of buildings newer than 2015, park trees. Landmark heights: CTBUH / Skyscraper Center, Wikipedia and operator figures. Google Maps was not consulted: the Chrome extension was not connected.

minimap.note: District names for the minimap (centres) and the tier-A landmarks to mark on it; the map itself draws from roads / water / parks / buildings. Screen up = -Z (north).

landmarks.name: Space Needle
landmarks.desc: The city's signature, built for the 1962 World's Fair. Three pairs of slender white steel legs (each pair a tapering hourglass of two curved columns, splayed at the base about 36 m apart and pinched to a waist at about 114 m, the 'wasp waist') rise from a round concrete base; between them a central core carries the glass elevators (gold-cabbed lifts visible running up the outside of the core). At 152-158 m sits the top house: a flying-saucer disc about 42 m across - a dark rotating restaurant floor ('The Loupe', glass floor) under the observation deck with its 2018 floor-to-ceiling glass barrier walls leaning outward, a white sunburst of halo-ring struts under the saucer, then the flat roof with the 'halo' ring and a short lantern spire and beacon to 184 m. Colours: white structure ('Astronaut White'), the saucer's underside and the 'halo' in white, the roof spire with the orange 'Galaxy Gold' accent on the sunburst. At the base the round Pavilion (glass, two storeys) and the spiral entry ramp. It must be liftable and tearable like any tower: tear at the waist.

landmarks.name: Climate Pledge Arena
landmarks.desc: The 1962 Washington State Coliseum (KeyArena), rebuilt 2021 under its listed roof. A square pavilion about 125 x 125 m: the green-patinated copper-clad roof is a hyperbolic-paraboloid saddle hung from four great concrete-and-steel trusses spanning corner to corner, its high points at the north and south corners (about 33 m) and low at east and west, the roof edge sweeping in a thin curved fascia. Under it, full-height glass curtain walls on all four sides, the sloping exterior concrete buttresses (the 'A-frame' supports at the corners) visible through the glass, the bowl sunk below ground so the building reads low. A living green wall at the north-west and the Atrium glass entry on the east toward the Fountain lawn.

landmarks.name: Museum of Pop Culture (MoPOP)
landmarks.desc: Frank Gehry, 2000. A cluster of six swollen, crumpled blob forms (said to be a smashed electric guitar) clad in about 21,000 shingled stainless-steel and aluminium panels in bright colours: gold, silver (bead blasted), deep magenta-purple, red, light blue, and an iridescent 'purple haze' piece that shifts colour. About 140 x 90 m, 15-26 m tall, no straight walls. The Monorail runs north-south straight through the building on its concrete beams (a slot in the blobs), and the 'Sky Church' hall sits under the tallest form. Front toward the Fountain lawn and the Armory to the west; the Space Needle stands just south-west.

landmarks.name: Pacific Science Center
landmarks.desc: Minoru Yamasaki's US Science Pavilion for the 1962 fair: five low white buildings with white precast 'Space Gothic' tracery (slender pointed-arch ribs) round a courtyard of shallow raised reflecting pools and walkways, and over the pools five free-standing white concrete lattice arches, each four slender ribs meeting in a pointed Gothic arch about 33 m tall. White and pale grey throughout, the pools a dark blue. About 150 x 110 m. Main entrance north toward the Armory and the Fountain; the IMAX dome (a white drum) at the south-east.

landmarks.name: Chihuly Garden and Glass
landmarks.desc: Directly at the Space Needle's west foot. The Glasshouse: a 12 m tall glass-and-steel conservatory about 30 m long whose roof is a sloping tilted ridge (inspired by the Crystal Palace and Sainte-Chapelle), hung inside with a 30 m long red / orange / amber / yellow glass flower sculpture. Beside it the garden: beds of dark planting with tall glass spears, reeds and spheres in saturated reds, blues, yellows, a lime-green glass forest, and the low dark exhibition hall. The glass should glint in the sun.

landmarks.name: International Fountain
landmarks.desc: A 67 m round bowl of white concrete stepping down in shallow rings to a hemispherical stainless-steel dome 9 m across studded with nozzles that throw water jets up to 37 m in choreographed bursts. Grass lawn all round (the 'Fountain lawn'). Fixed prop; kaiju can stomp the jets.

landmarks.name: Seattle Center Armory
landmarks.desc: 1939 Art Moderne National Guard armory (the 'Center House' food hall): a long pale grey concrete hall about 110 x 90 m, flat roof, tall vertical window bands, a glazed north front onto the Fountain lawn.

landmarks.name: McCaw Hall
landmarks.desc: Opera house (2003) on Mercer St: a tall glass lobby wall with red and violet scrims and a curved metal roof over a tan stucco box; front faces south across the Kreielsheimer Promenade.

landmarks.name: Gates Foundation campus
landmarks.desc: Two long six-storey boomerang-shaped glass-and-limestone office wings (2011) over a planted courtyard and reflecting pool, east of Seattle Center across 5th Ave N.

landmarks.name: Seattle Center Monorail
landmarks.desc: The 1962 Alweg straddle-beam monorail, 1.4 km from Westlake Center (a station on the 3rd floor over 5th Ave and Pine St) up the middle of 5th Ave, curving at 5th and Denny onto the cardinal grid, north through MoPOP to the Seattle Center station by the Armory. Two parallel pre-stressed concrete beams (0.9 m wide x 1.5 m deep, about 4.5 m apart) on single T-shaped concrete columns about 6-9 m tall at roughly 30 m spacing; the beams are light grey concrete. Trains (prop 'monorail_train'): two four-car articulated units about 37 m long, 3 m wide, 4 m tall, with rounded noses, wrap-round windows and a silver aluminium lower skirt that hugs the beam; one Blue, one Red. The layout's monorail polylines (layout.monorail) carry the beam centrelines.

landmarks.name: Monorail train
landmarks.desc: One of the two 1962 Alweg trains (Red, Blue): four articulated cars 37 m long overall, a rounded bullet-nosed cab at each end with a wrap-round windscreen, ribbon windows, white / silver body with a deep red (or blue) band and skirt that straddles the concrete beam. Placed on the beam polylines.

landmarks.name: Columbia Center
landmarks.desc: 701 Fifth Ave (between Columbia and Cherry St), the tallest building in the Pacific Northwest, 1985. Plan: three concave-faced lobes nested round a core, each lobe a stack of convex and concave facets, so the tower reads as a cluster of three tall shafts that step down at different heights (the north lobe highest) - setbacks at the 43rd and 76th floors. Facade: polished black granite at the base, the shaft in very dark, almost black, glass with thin black mullions (it reads black against the sky). Flat roof with the observatory (Sky View, 73rd floor). Base: a granite podium stepping down the steep hill along Columbia St, entrance plaza on Fifth Ave. Footprint about 52 x 54 m.

landmarks.name: Seattle Municipal Tower
landmarks.desc: 700 Fifth Ave (1990), across Fifth Ave east of Columbia Center. Blue-green and teal reflective glass with darker horizontal bands; the plan is a rectangle with stepped, chamfered bays and a curved rounded front toward Fifth Ave, the mass stepping back in tiers near the top (setbacks with green glass) to a flat-topped crown with two small fins. The base steps down the hill toward Fourth Ave. About 58 x 40 m.

landmarks.name: F5 Tower
landmarks.desc: 801 Fifth Ave at Marion St (2017, 'The Mark' tower). A 44-storey glass tower whose curtain wall is folded and faceted: the plan widens upward (inverted-taper corners) and the facades are broken into large tilted glass planes, silver-blue reflective glass with fine white mullions. At its foot on Fifth Ave the preserved 1910 First United Methodist Church: a domed Beaux-Arts sanctuary in buff brick and terracotta with a large copper-green dome (about 25 m), now an event hall - include it as part of the model.

landmarks.name: Rainier Square Tower
landmarks.desc: On Fourth Ave at Union St, the north half of the Rainier Square block (2020, 58 storeys). Silver-grey glass with a shingled curtain wall of vertical bands. Its west face (Fourth Ave) slopes in a long concave curve: the tower is widest at about the 10th floor and the facade bows back as it rises, a gesture echoing Rainier Tower's tapered pedestal next door; the other faces are flat. Flat top with a slightly raked crown. The low podium holds a hotel and the Amazon Go store. About 50 x 35 m. (Which face carries the curve is from memory: check it against a photo before modelling.)

landmarks.name: Rainier Tower
landmarks.desc: Minoru Yamasaki, 1977, at Fifth Ave and University St. A 29-storey square office shaft (about 33 x 33 m) of light aluminium and narrow bronze-tinted windows (Yamasaki's tight vertical stripes) standing on an inverted, tapered 11-storey concrete pedestal: the pedestal is about 12 m square at the ground and flares out in four smooth white concave curves to the full tower width at about 37 m up - the building looks like a golf tee. The tear must start at the pedestal.

landmarks.name: 1201 Third Avenue
landmarks.desc: 1988 postmodern tower (formerly Washington Mutual Tower) on Third Ave between Seneca and University. A square plan with deeply notched (stepped) corners; light grey-pink granite piers framing bands of blue-green reflective glass. It steps in at the top in a series of setbacks to a stepped pyramidal crown, the glass becoming a lit lantern; the crown is white-lit at night. About 46 x 46 m.

landmarks.name: Two Union Square
landmarks.desc: 601 Union St (1989), east of Sixth Ave above Freeway Park. Its plan is a square with scalloped, concave faces between rounded chamfered corners (a fluted cross), clad in blue-green reflective glass with fine horizontal mullions; the top floors step back on the concave faces to a slanted, flat crown. About 46 x 46 m. Its low neighbour One Union Square (worn concrete, 1981) stands to the west.

landmarks.name: JPMorganChase Center (Russell Investments Center)
landmarks.desc: 1301 Second Ave (2006, 42 storeys), above the Seattle Art Museum's expansion. A plain rectangular slab (about 60 x 34 m) of clear silver-grey glass with thin aluminium fins, its long faces toward the bay and the hill; the flat top has a glass mechanical screen. The lower 16 floors are SAM's galleries (glass with a limestone base on First Ave).

landmarks.name: U.S. Bank Centre
landmarks.desc: 1420 Fifth Ave at Pike St (1989). Postmodern: pinkish-brown granite and dark green-blue glass in a square plan with deeply stepped (sawtooth) corners, bay windows of glass between granite piers; at the top the stepped corners rise past the main roof into four small granite spires framing a lit glass lantern crown. Pacific Place and the Nordstrom flagship are across the street.

landmarks.name: Seattle Central Library
landmarks.desc: OMA / Rem Koolhaas, 2004, the block between Fourth and Fifth Ave, Madison and Spring St. Five stacked floor platforms shifted off one another, wrapped in a single skin of glass in a steel diamond grid (diagrid of about 3 x 3.6 m diamonds, silver-grey steel, the glass partly with expanded-metal interlayer so it reads silver-blue): the skin slopes and folds between the platforms - overhangs cantilever over Fourth Ave and over Fifth Ave, a sloping glass face drops down to the Fourth Ave plaza. 11 storeys, about 56 m high; the hill makes Fifth Ave two floors higher than Fourth. Bright yellow escalators and the red 'red floor' show through the glass.

landmarks.name: Smith Tower
landmarks.desc: 506 Second Ave at Yesler Way, Pioneer Square (1914), once the tallest building west of the Mississippi. A 21-storey base block about 33 x 33 m and a slimmer 14-storey tower set on its west half to the 35th floor (the Chinese Room observatory with its open balcony), then a steep pointed pyramid roof of green-white glazed terracotta to a glass-globe lantern at 148 m. White glazed terracotta over the whole facade (bright white with pale cream), tall arched windows at the top of the base, a granite ground floor with a grand entrance on Second Ave.

landmarks.name: Pike Place Market (Main Arcade)
landmarks.desc: The 1907 public market on the bluff above the waterfront, Pike Place at the foot of Pike St. The Main Arcade and Economy Market: a long low arcade (the layout lot is 129 x 35 m along the west side of Pike Place, its south end under the sign at Pike St) of whitewashed timber posts, hanging produce stalls under a wide shed roof open to the street, white-painted brick upper facades with green trim and red lettering, stepping down five levels at the back to Western Ave. On the corner at Pike St and Pike Place: the iconic red neon 'PUBLIC MARKET CENTER' sign on a frame above the roof, the 'FARMERS MARKET' lettering, and the round clock (white face, red neon ring) on its post - prop 'pike_place_sign'. Rachel the bronze piggy bank under the sign; the Market's brick streets in front.

landmarks.name: Public Market Center sign and clock
landmarks.desc: The red neon sign 'PUBLIC MARKET CENTER' (about 18 m of tall red letters on a steel frame, white outlines) above the Main Arcade roof at the foot of Pike St, with 'MEET THE PRODUCER' / 'FARMERS MARKET' boards below and the round 1927 market clock on its tall post in front (white face, red neon numerals and ring). Faces up Pike St (ENE). Glows at dusk.

landmarks.name: Westlake Center
landmarks.desc: Fourth to Fifth Ave at Pine St (1988). A four-storey shopping mall in pale granite and green glass with a glass atrium and a curved glass corner to Westlake Park, and on the Fifth Ave side the 25-storey office tower (grey granite and green glass bands). The Monorail's south terminal is on the mall's third floor: the twin beams end in the building over Fifth Ave.

landmarks.name: Seattle Convention Center Summit
landmarks.desc: Summit building (2023), Pine St to Olive Way at Ninth Ave / Boren. A big five-level box of exhibition halls with a striking facade of large stacked, sloping glass and terracotta-coloured panels and diagonal glass cuts; a huge glazed lobby stair on Pine St; a forest of panels, rhythmic and warm. The older Arch building (1988) spans I-5 at Pike St and Seventh Ave over Freeway Park.

landmarks.name: Seattle Art Museum
landmarks.desc: Venturi Scott Brown, 1991, on First Ave at University St, the block stepping down the hill. A limestone facade of huge carved letters 'SEATTLE ART MUSEUM', fluted cream limestone with arched openings and bands of red-orange terracotta, pink-and-grey granite courses, and the 'Grand Stairway' along University St. In front on the First Ave corner stands Hammering Man (prop 'hammering_man').

landmarks.name: Hammering Man
landmarks.desc: Jonathan Borofsky's 14.6 m flat black steel silhouette of a worker whose motorised arm swings a hammer slowly up and down, on the First Ave sidewalk in front of SAM, facing the street.

landmarks.name: Seattle Great Wheel
landmarks.desc: A 53 m (175 ft) white steel observation wheel (2012) at the outer end of Pier 57, partly over the water. A slim white rim truss with 42 enclosed gondolas (white with silver-blue tinted glass, one VIP gondola red with a glass floor), radial spokes in white cable, a white A-frame on each side carrying the hub, the base on the pier deck. The wheel's plane lies across the pier (it faces the bay and the city; check the orientation against a photo). Lit with LED patterns at night. onPier: it stands on the pier, not on land.

landmarks.name: Pier 57 (Miners Landing)
landmarks.desc: A 1902 timber pier shed (about 120 m along the pier x 30 m): grey-weathered board-and-batten walls, a low gabled roof with a clerestory, large painted 'MINERS LANDING' and 'PIER 57' signs on the street end facing Alaskan Way, a vintage carousel inside, the deck on timber piles over the water. The Great Wheel stands at its outer end.

landmarks.name: Seattle Aquarium
landmarks.desc: The aquarium on Pier 59 (1977): a long pier shed with a restored 1905 Beaux-Arts style street front (white-and-cream arched bays with the AQUARIUM letters) on Alaskan Way, timber and glass behind it, the outer end with the harbour-seal and otter pools. Across Alaskan Way at the foot of the Overlook Walk the Ocean Pavilion (2024): a round two-storey drum clad in dark, rippled wave-patterned panels with a planted roof terrace - include it as part of the landmark or as its own B piece (ocean_pavilion).

landmarks.name: Seattle Aquarium Ocean Pavilion
landmarks.desc: 2024 round pavilion (about 50 m across) of rough dark grey stone-like panels with a planted roof that becomes part of the Overlook Walk, east side of Alaskan Way opposite Pier 59.

landmarks.name: Overlook Walk
landmarks.desc: 2024 sloping pedestrian bridge-park from Pike Place Market down over Alaskan Way to the waterfront: wide planted terraces and concrete steps, wood benches, glass rails, ending in an amphitheatre stair by the Aquarium. Treat as a raised plaza on columns over the road.

landmarks.name: Colman Dock (Seattle Ferry Terminal)
landmarks.desc: Washington State Ferries' Pier 52 terminal (rebuilt 2017-2023). The broad timber-and-concrete pier (about 250 x 150 m) is mostly vehicle holding lanes; the new terminal building at its north-east is two storeys of glass under a long timber-beamed canopy roof sloping toward the bay, with a public plaza and the elevated walkway to Marion St. Three ferry slips on the west face with steel towers (white-and-green slip towers with counterweights) and wooden dolphins; the King County water-taxi float on the south. One WSF ferry (prop 'wsf_ferry') sits in the middle slip.

landmarks.name: Washington State Ferry (Jumbo Mark II)
landmarks.desc: A Jumbo Mark II class double-ended ferry (MV Wenatchee / Tacoma / Puyallup), 140 m long and 27 m wide: a white superstructure with two passenger decks of long window bands, a dark green hull and green trim stripe, the WSF logo, two bridge cabins (one at each end), two buff funnels with the green and white WSF band, open car decks at both ends. Lies in the slip with its long axis along the pier (WSW-ENE).

landmarks.name: Washington State Ferry (under way)
landmarks.desc: A second ferry crossing Elliott Bay toward Bainbridge Island (same model as wsf_ferry), heading WSW.

landmarks.name: Pier 54 (Ivar's Acres of Clams)
landmarks.desc: 1900s pier shed with a bright white clapboard front, a red-and-white 'IVAR'S ACRES OF CLAMS' sign, gabled roof, open deck at the end.

landmarks.name: Pier 62
landmarks.desc: Open public pier (rebuilt 2020): a bare deck of light concrete and grated panels on piles with a steel railing; used for events.

landmarks.name: Pier 66 (Bell Street Pier)
landmarks.desc: The Port's Bell Street Pier (1996): conference centre and cruise terminal in pale green-grey panels with a curved roof and a tall glass rotunda, a small marina basin to its north.

landmarks.name: The Edgewater
landmarks.desc: Pier 67 hotel: a four-storey timber lodge-style building over the water, brown shingles and green trim.

landmarks.name: Pier 69 (Port of Seattle)
landmarks.desc: The Port of Seattle headquarters, a long white converted pier warehouse with blue trim; the Victoria Clipper catamarans dock along it.

landmarks.name: Olympic Sculpture Park
landmarks.desc: SAM's 3.6 ha park (2007, Weiss/Manfredi): a Z-shaped green ramp descending 12 m from the PACCAR Pavilion (glass-fronted, planted roof) at Western Ave and Broad St, bridging over Elliott Ave and the BNSF railway to the shore and a pocket beach. Lawns, meadows and aspen grove, folded concrete retaining walls. Sculptures (props): Alexander Calder's 'The Eagle' (11.9 m, bright red-orange steel, on the upper terrace, framing the Space Needle), Richard Serra's 'Wake' (five 4 m weathering-steel S-curves), Jaume Plensa's 'Echo' (a 14.6 m white elongated girl's head on the shore facing the bay), Louise Bourgeois' 'Father and Son' fountain, Claes Oldenburg's 'Typewriter Eraser' (orange disc and blue brush).

landmarks.name: The Eagle (Calder)
landmarks.desc: Alexander Calder's 1971 stabile: three-legged swooping bright red-orange painted steel plates, 11.9 m.

landmarks.name: Echo (Plensa)
landmarks.desc: Jaume Plensa's 14.6 m white marble-resin elongated girl's head with closed eyes, on the shore facing the bay.

landmarks.name: Lumen Field
landmarks.desc: The Seahawks / Sounders stadium (2002, 68,000), between Occidental Ave S and the railway. A horseshoe bowl about 270 x 230 m, open to the north end (where the stands drop to frame the downtown skyline and the north plaza), the two long sidelines covered by cantilevered roofs of steel and polycarbonate hung from two enormous white tri-chord tubular steel arches ('rainbow trusses') that run the length of each sideline and rise to 79 m above the field. The layout lot (230 x 270 m) is the bowl only; the Event Center south of it stays a generic building. Facade: exposed grey steel and concrete ramps, blue-green glass, the 'Hawks Nest' end low. The field is green artificial turf with the Seahawks logo; the stadium's Event Center (a big low exhibition hall) and parking garage adjoin on the south.

landmarks.name: T-Mobile Park
landmarks.desc: The Mariners' ballpark (1999, 47,000), south of Lumen Field between First Ave S and the railway, with home plate at the south-west corner (main 'Home Plate' entrance at Edgar Martinez Dr and First Ave S, a red-brick and green-steel facade with a clock) and the outfield opening north-east toward downtown. Its retractable roof: three huge curved steel panels that ride on wheeled trucks along rails on top of the stands and, when open, stack over the railway east of the park (the roof stands on its own gantry of exposed green steel trusses, 65 m to the top). Red brick, dark green steel, natural grass field.

landmarks.name: King Street Station
landmarks.desc: 1906 railway station (Reed and Stem) at Second Ave S and S Jackson St. A long three-storey red-brick building with cast-stone and terracotta trim along the tracks, and at its north-west corner the 74 m (242 ft) clock tower modelled on the Campanile of St Mark's in Venice: a square red-brick shaft with four large white clock faces near the top under a pierced belfry, a pyramidal roof and finial. The grand stair and plaza on Jackson St (north); the station sits at the platform level below.

landmarks.name: Union Station
landmarks.desc: 1911 Beaux-Arts station on S Jackson St at Fourth Ave S, east of King Street Station: a symmetrical red-brick and cream terracotta block about 90 x 45 m dominated by a huge arched window on the north front, under a long barrel-vaulted grand hall roof (copper-green), small corner pavilions, a glass canopy entrance. Now Sound Transit's offices; the Union Station square and the light-rail tunnel portal beside it.

landmarks.name: Pioneer Building
landmarks.desc: 1892 Romanesque Revival office block at First Ave and Yesler Way: six storeys of red-brown brick and sandstone, a deep arched entrance, bay windows, a cornice; across the triangle the Pioneer Place pergola (prop 'pioneer_pergola').

landmarks.name: Pioneer Square pergola and totem pole
landmarks.desc: The 1909 cast-iron and glass pergola (an ornate Victorian bus shelter, about 18 m long, black ironwork, glass roof) in the triangular Pioneer Place, with the 18 m Tlingit totem pole (carved red, black and white figures) beside it and a bust of Chief Seattle.

landmarks.name: King County Courthouse
landmarks.desc: 1916-31 granite-and-brick courthouse filling a block on Third Ave, 12 storeys, classical piers.

landmarks.name: Chinatown Gate
landmarks.desc: 2008 paifang on S King St at Fifth Ave S: red columns, a green glazed-tile roof with upturned eaves, gold characters; faces west toward the stations.

landmarks.name: Arctic Building
landmarks.desc: 1917 terracotta office block at Third and Cherry, eight storeys of cream glazed terracotta with a row of terracotta walrus heads round the third floor and a dark blue-glazed upper band.

landmarks.name: The Spheres
landmarks.desc: Amazon's three intersecting glass domes (2018) at Sixth Ave and Lenora St: three spheres (the largest 39.6 m across and 27.4 m tall, the others about 30 m and 24 m) built as pentagonal hexecontahedra - a steel lattice of five-pointed star / kite shapes ('Catalan solid') in dark grey steel with about 2,600 clear glass panes, packed with a tropical cloud forest inside (green visible through the glass). They sit on a low plinth in a plaza between Doppler and Day 1; at night they glow warm.

landmarks.name: Doppler
landmarks.desc: Amazon's first Denny Triangle tower (2015), 2021 Seventh Ave: 37 storeys of blue-grey glass with a faceted, rhythmic pattern of slightly offset glass bays and horizontal aluminium bands; a low podium with the Amazon Go store; flat top with a glass screen.

landmarks.name: Day 1
landmarks.desc: Amazon's Day 1 tower (2016), 2121 Seventh Ave across Lenora St from Doppler: 37 storeys of grey-blue glass with the same offset-bay pattern, the Spheres at its foot. With Doppler and the Spheres it is the Amazon campus card.

landmarks.name: Hyatt Regency Seattle
landmarks.desc: 2018, the largest hotel in the Pacific Northwest: 45 storeys of blue-grey glass, a long slim slab with rounded ends at Eighth Ave and Howell St.

landmarks.name: The Westin Seattle
landmarks.desc: Two cylindrical hotel towers (1969 and 1982) of white precast concrete with continuous horizontal window bands ('corn cob' towers), at Fifth Ave and Westlake, the Monorail passing in front.

landmarks.name: William Kenzo Nakamura US Courthouse
landmarks.desc: 2004 federal courthouse at Seventh Ave and Stewart St: 23 storeys of glass and white metal with a thin projecting curved roof blade.

landmarks.name: Safeco Plaza
landmarks.desc: 1001 Fourth Ave (1969): a dark bronze-brown steel-and-glass box, 50 storeys, with continuous vertical mullions; the Henry Moore 'Three Piece Sculpture: Vertebrae' on its plaza.

landmarks.name: Docusign Tower (Wells Fargo Center)
landmarks.desc: 999 Third Ave (1983): 47 storeys of grey granite and bronze glass with notched corners and a flat top.

landmarks.name: Fourth & Madison
landmarks.desc: 2002: 40 storeys of green-tinted glass and tan precast with a curved, pitched glass crown.

landmarks.name: Bank of America Fifth Avenue Plaza
landmarks.desc: 800 Fifth Ave (1981): dark tinted glass and white-grey bands, 42 storeys.

landmarks.name: 1000 Second Avenue
landmarks.desc: 1987: 40 storeys of light pink granite and blue glass with stepped octagonal setbacks.

landmarks.name: Seattle Tower
landmarks.desc: 1928 Art Deco (Northern Life Tower) at Third Ave and University St: 27 storeys of brick shading from dark brown at the base to light buff at the top (said to evoke a mountain), stepped setbacks, vertical piers, a stepped crown.

landmarks.name: Qualtrics Tower (2+U)
landmarks.desc: 2021, Second Ave and University St: a 38-storey glass tower lifted on huge diagonal-braced columns over a three-storey open public 'urban porch'.

landmarks.name: Fairmont Olympic Hotel
landmarks.desc: 1924 Italian Renaissance hotel, a U-shaped block of tan brick and cream terracotta with an arched loggia.

landmarks.name: Benaroya Hall
landmarks.desc: 1998 concert hall on Third Ave at Union: a curved glass lobby drum (the Samuel and Althea Stroum Grand Lobby) in front of the limestone-clad hall.

landmarks.name: Paramount Theatre
landmarks.desc: 1928 movie palace at Ninth Ave and Pine St: a tall buff brick block with a vertical red neon PARAMOUNT blade sign and a marquee.

landmarks.name: Nordstrom flagship
landmarks.desc: The old Frederick & Nelson store (1918), Fifth to Sixth Ave at Pine: six storeys of cream terracotta with arched windows.

landmarks.name: Bon Marche Building
landmarks.desc: 1929 Art Deco department store filling the block at Third Ave and Pine St, buff brick with green-bronze spandrels and a big clock at the corner.

landmarks.name: Moore Theatre
landmarks.desc: 1907 theatre and hotel at Second Ave and Virginia St, white glazed terracotta with a vertical sign.

landmarks.name: Cinerama
landmarks.desc: 1963 Cinerama movie house at Fourth Ave and Lenora: a curved white wall with the big neon sign.

landmarks.name: Victor Steinbrueck Park
landmarks.desc: Lawn on the bluff at the north end of the Market with two 15 m red-cedar totem poles and a view over the bay.

landmarks.name: Museum of History & Industry
landmarks.desc: The 1942 Naval Reserve Armory at Lake Union Park, on the south shore of Lake Union: a long Streamline Moderne white concrete hall with a tall glazed north front and a stepped tower. Wooden-boat docks and the Center for Wooden Boats float beside it.

landmarks.name: KEXP / Northwest Rooms
landmarks.desc: Low 1962 fair buildings on the north side of Seattle Center, the KEXP radio studio with its big window.

ring.title: EMERALD CITY HEAVYWEIGHT CHAMPIONSHIP
ring.note: Title Match ring on Terminal 46, the Port of Seattle's open paved apron on the waterfront between the stadiums and Elliott Bay (south of Colman Dock and Pier 48, west of Alaskan Way / SR 99 and the railway). Lumen Field and T-Mobile Park stand just east, the downtown skyline (Columbia Center, Smith Tower) rises to the north-north-east and the Space Needle beyond it; the bay, West Seattle and the Olympics are behind the west side. The owner's first choice, the International Fountain lawn at Seattle Center, cannot take the Chicago venue: its box would hold nine landmarks (see alternatives). venueBox [minX, minZ, maxX, maxZ] = Chicago venue x -58..+48 (west edge pulled in by ring.west = 12 u, chicago_arena SITE.west), z -78..+78 with both grandstands; runwayBox = the entrance runway and gate (ring.east = 10 u keeps them short of Lumen Field) about the ring centre without grandstands; venueWaterShare = the part of that box over the bay. The east edge reaches the Alaskan Way / SR 99 ramps and the railway (roads under the venue are clipped as on NYC). removedSmallStructures (port sheds and booths, all low) are left out of the layout and seattle_trees.json leaves out every tree within ringClearTrees. clear = half-size of the largest axis-aligned square free of buildings and props.

alternatives.note: Seattle Center, the International Fountain lawn (the owner's first choice): the venue box would take nine landmarks (Climate Pledge Arena, the Armory, MoPOP, McCaw Hall, KEXP, the Gates Foundation, Chihuly Garden and Glass, the Space Needle, the fountain itself). Not usable without removing landmarks.
Seattle Center shifted west over Climate Pledge Arena / the Key lots: still takes the arena and the Armory. Not usable.
Terminal 46 north end (Pier 46 / the stadium north lots): the box reaches the Alaskan Way / SR 99 ramps and the ferry holding lanes; workable but the chosen site sits on more open apron.

a.note: player (seattle-integrator, lead-authorised; passes kaijuDuel.js spawnIsClear with 11u): east edge of Seattle Center by the Gates Foundation, the Space Needle and MoPOP behind

b.note: rival (seattle-integrator, lead-authorised): the lawn on Alaskan Way South by Pioneer Square, Smith Tower and the Pioneer Building behind

duel.note: VS Duel: the two kaiju face each other down the length of downtown, about 491 u apart (kaijuDuel.js findDuelSpawns searches +-60 u round each).

soldier.note: Lone Soldier start: Pike St at First Ave, facing west-south-west down the street at the Pike Place Market's red PUBLIC MARKET CENTER sign and clock, the bay and the Olympics beyond; the towers of the core rise behind.
